title: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard -- Ch. 12: Counting Automated Ballots: Which Rules Apply?
keywords: Counting Automated Ballots: Which Rules Apply?

600 public school teachers of Pasay City
primary_topics: Chapter 12 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- CJP's lengthy Dissenting Opinion in Loong v. Comelec, arguing that automated ballots cast in an automated election cannot lawfully be counted by hand under the Omnibus Election Code's rules for handwritten ballots, and that the Comelec gravely abused its discretion in abandoning the automated count in Sulu

A detailed exposition of the Philippine automated election system under RA 8436 -- pre-printed ballots with shaded ovals, optical scanning machines, twenty-three statutory features, audit trails, minimum human intervention, and counting at a central counting center rather than in the precincts

A full factual reconstruction of the May 1998 ARMM elections in Sulu: the three PATA ballots that triggered Atty. Jose Tolentino Jr.'s province-wide suspension of the machine count at 65 percent completion, the misprinted ovals and wrong sequence codes, the airlift of ballot boxes and machines by C130 to the PICC, and the purely manual count by Pasay City teachers on which Abdusakur Tan was proclaimed governor

His five grounds of grave abuse -- peremptory stoppage, the unproven threat of violence, the Comelec's disobedience of its own parallel-count Resolution, the use of manual-election rules on automated ballots, and the issuance of the Minute Resolutions without notice or hearing -- and his proposed remedy of a special election for governor only

His larger warning that upholding the manual count sets back election modernization, rewards losing candidates who allege a few miscounts, and usurps the legislature's role, since only Congress may supply the remedy RA 8436 failed to provide
sub_topics: He opens with the premise that honest, credible and peaceful elections at regular intervals are the backbone of representative democracy, contrasting Philippine fraud, terrorism and delay with results announced within hours in mature democracies

He traces the country's election woes to an antiquated manual system susceptible to machination and fraud, which led Congress to adopt automation through RA 8436, enacted December 22, 1997 and first used in the ARMM on May 11, 1998

He describes the system's core features: machine-generated results and minimum human intervention, pre-printed ballots whose ovals the voter shades, optical scanning machines that count and reject fake ballots, and the removal of BEI discretion in appreciating ballots

He reproduces Section 7 of RA 8436 in full, listing the twenty-three required features from built-in multi-layer security and audit trails to fake-ballot rejectors, 100-150 ballots per minute, and a guaranteed, warranted margin of error

He explains the ARMM mechanics: separate national and local ballots printed by the National Printing Office on special paper, unique machine-printed sequence codes per municipality, and the Comelec's provision of only one ballot box per precinct in Sulu despite the law's requirement of two

He sets out the prescribed counting and canvassing procedure -- sealed boxes taken to a counting center, excess ballots drawn at random, seven printed copies of the election return, diskettes consolidated by the boards of canvassers, and proclamation by the Comelec en banc and by Congress in joint session

He narrates the trigger: at about 6:00 a.m. on May 12, 1998, watchers complained of discrepancies in PATA returns, and Atty. Tolentino personally pulled three counted ballots showing votes not credited to a mayoralty candidate

He recounts that technical experts traced the fault to misaligned ovals in the printing of the local ballots, and that Tolentino ordered a province-wide suspension, followed by a Camp General Bautista conference where two generals, a police director and three candidates split over manual versus automated counting

He reproduces Tolentino's handwritten fax report, which cited a machine with an error rate of 1:1,000,000 and urged staying away from 'a lifeless thing that has sown tension and anxiety among and between the voters of Sulu'

He follows the chain of Comelec Minute Resolutions -- 98-1747 for a PATA manual count, 98-1750 airlifting machines and boards to the PICC, 98-1796 adding a parallel manual count in all eighteen municipalities, and 98-1798 fixing the PICC procedure

He records Loong's objections, the Court's status quo order suspending Tan's proclamation, and the fact that the Comelec, for inexplicable reasons, held only a manual count by public school teachers in Pasay City, on which Tan was proclaimed with 43,573 votes

He summarizes the nine grounds of the majority opinion by Justice Reynato S. Puno: a grossly erroneous count was inevitable, a bloodbath was averted, no denial of due process, ballot integrity preserved, a reliable count that Tan's own allies mostly lost, non-machine errors, no statutory prohibition on manual counting, no failure of election under Section 6 of the Omnibus Election Code, and the movement toward empowering the Comelec

He states his first ground of dissent: the stoppage was legally and factually flawed, since Tolentino admitted at the September 25, 1998 Oral Argument that he had no statutory or regulatory basis, acted on three ballots out of about 200 in one of PATA's 27 precincts, and never checked whether those votes could change the result

He argues the proper remedy for questionable returns was objection during canvassing, a pre-proclamation controversy under Section 243 of the OEC as amended by RA 7166, or an election protest -- not stoppage of the count in all eighteen municipalities when errors appeared in only six

He disputes the imminent-violence justification, citing the PNP provincial director's Comprehensive Report of May 18, 1998, which described a generally peaceful election with less cheating than before, and notes that even a real threat would justify only a change of venue, not the 'manualization' of the count

He shows the Comelec disobeyed its own Resolution 98-1796 by never conducting the ordered automated count, abandoning without explanation a process already 65 percent complete and substituting its own will for that of Congress

He demonstrates through the Court-ordered February 9, 1999 physical examination that manual and machine appreciation diverge systematically -- ink-shaded ovals, partly shaded ovals, crossed-out ovals read as over-votes, and handwritten names treated as marks -- so the manual count could not reflect the automated count

He warns that human handling of automated ballots invites fraud, since blank ballots can be pencil-marked and votes nullified by shading a rival's oval, and that upholding the manual count would give candidates a degenerated means to delay proclamations and defeat the modernization Congress ordained

He finds a denial of due process: the Tolentino meeting was post facto and limited to PATA, and Minute Resolution 98-1747 was issued the same day without notice, hearing or independent investigation, relying entirely on Tan's petition

He concludes in his Epilogue that a void order yields a void count, that an automated recount had become impossible because handled ballots were blemished, and that the only equitable remedy is a special election limited to the governorship, other candidates having accepted the results

He ends with a call for legislative action, since RA 8436 left a lacuna for non-machine errors that courts and the Comelec have no power to fill without committing judicial or administrative legislation contrary to separation of powers
He closes with the typewriter-and-computer analogy and the judgment that time will tell whether the Court applied a Jurassic-age solution to a third-millennium problem

stances.claim: Automated ballots cast during an automated election cannot be counted manually under the Omnibus Election Code's rules for handwritten ballots; they can be counted only under the rules of the Automated Election Law, RA 8436.
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-matching argument driven to a technology analogy -- a typewriter and a computer both make text, but their rules cannot be interchanged

stances.claim: The Comelec gravely abused its discretion by stopping a count that was 65 percent complete on the strength of three ballots from one precinct, by shifting to a manual count on an unsubstantiated threat of violence, by disobeying its own Resolution requiring an automated count, and by issuing the assailed Minute Resolutions without notice, hearing or investigation.
stances.rhetorical_move: itemized indictment, each ground traced to the record, the Oral Argument admission and the PNP's own peaceful-election report

stances.claim: The manual count could not reflect the machine count, because the BEIs validated ink-shaded and partly shaded ovals the machines ignored, counted uncrossed votes the machines read as over-votes, and treated written names as marks -- so the results substantially differed.
stances.rhetorical_move: empirical demonstration from the Court-ordered physical examination, listing the specific classes of divergence

stances.claim: Because the void Resolutions yielded no valid count and an automated recount was no longer possible, the only equitable remedy was a special election limited to the governorship of Sulu, so the people's true choice could be expressed.
stances.rhetorical_move: remedial reasoning bounded by who sought relief -- other candidates, having not objected, are deemed to have accepted the results

stances.claim: RA 8436 left a gap for errors unrelated to the machines, and neither the courts nor the Comelec may fill that vacuum; only Congress can prescribe the remedy, since anything else is judicial or administrative legislation contrary to separation of powers.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional restraint: identifying a lacuna and assigning it to the legislature rather than resolving it by construction

stances.claim: Upholding the manual count sets back election modernization, because it hands losing candidates an easy device to scuttle automation by alleging a few miscounted ballots and to revive an antiquated, fraud-ridden method.
stances.rhetorical_move: slippery-slope warning tied to the statute's purpose of speed and accuracy

notable_anecdotes: He discloses that he spent many days and long hours of analysis, reflection and prayer writing his dissent, because automated elections were wholly new to the Court.

He recounts that the whole province-wide stoppage began when Atty. Tolentino, prompted by watchers, plucked out three already-counted PATA ballots and saw that a mayoralty candidate's votes were printed as zero.

He reproduces Tolentino's handwritten midnight fax, which admitted uncertainty whether the extra Marines at the Sulu State College were to tame a crowd or to make 'a show of force,' and urged staying away from a lifeless machine that had sown tension.

He describes the Camp General Bautista conference where two brigadier generals, the provincial police director and candidates Tan and the Tulawies favored a manual count while Loong and Jikiri wanted the automation to continue.

He notes the extraordinary logistics: two C130s carrying all the ballot boxes and counting machines plus 72 escort-watchers from Sulu to the PICC, and a third flying in the provincial board of canvassers.
He points out that Tolentino candidly admitted during the September 25, 1998 Oral Argument that he had no statutory or even regulatory basis for ordering the stoppage.

He recalls the majority's own reliance on the fact that 600 public school teachers of Pasay City had no difficulty reading the ballots with the naked eye, and answers with the results of the Court-ordered ballot examination of February 9, 1999.
He borrows from then Vice President Joseph E. Estrada the line that automation, prescribed as the cure for electoral fraud, could in imprudent hands prove worse than the disease.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' reproduced and explained CJP's lengthy Dissenting Opinion in Loong v. Comelec, the first case to test the Philippine automated election system. He began by describing how repeated fraud and delay in manual balloting led Congress to enact RA 8436 on December 22, 1997, and how the law's automated system -- pre-printed ballots with shaded ovals, optical scanning machines, audit trails, minimum human intervention and twenty-three statutory features -- was first used in the ARMM on May 11, 1998. He then reconstructed the Sulu controversy in detail: at dawn on May 12, watchers complained about PATA returns, Atty. Jose Tolentino Jr. pulled three already-counted ballots showing votes credited as zero, traced the fault to misaligned ovals in the printing of the local ballots, and suspended the automated count across the entire province when it was already 65 percent complete; the Comelec en banc then issued a chain of Minute Resolutions airlifting ballots, machines and canvassers by C130 to the PICC and ordering a parallel manual count, but in the end conducted only a manual count by public school teachers in Pasay City, on which Abdusakur Tan was proclaimed governor. Justice Reynato S. Puno's majority upheld the Comelec on nine grounds, including the avoidance of a bloodbath and the reliability of the hand count. CJP dissented on five grounds: the stoppage rested on three ballots and on an official who admitted he had no legal authority; the threat of violence was contradicted by the PNP's own report and would at most justify a change of venue, not of method; the Comelec disobeyed its own Resolution requiring an automated count; the BEIs appreciated automated ballots by Omnibus Election Code rules, producing systematic divergences from the machine count; and the Resolutions issued without notice or hearing denied due process. He concluded that a void order yields a void count, that the only equitable remedy was a special election for governor alone, that only Congress could fill the law's gap without judicial or administrative legislation, and that time would tell whether the Court had applied a Jurassic-age solution to a third-millennium problem.
